<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w05">{"year":1,"week":5,"id":"y1w05","title":"Operations, Decimals and Inverses of Fractions","subtitle":"Solving problems with fractions and mixed numbers; place value; changing between fractions, decimals and percentages; recurring decimals; additive and multiplicative inverses.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers in real-life problems.","Change fractions to decimals, and terminating or recurring decimals to fractions.","Use place value to read and write decimals.","Find additive and multiplicative inverses and say when they exist.","Move between fractions, decimals and percentages."],"keywords":["mixed number","common denominator","reciprocal","place value","terminating decimal","recurring decimal","additive inverse","multiplicative inverse","percentage"],"notes":[{"title":"Fractions are numbers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A fraction $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ means $a\\div b$, provided $b\\neq0$. The same number can be written in several ways:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{3}{4}=\\frac{6}{8}=0.75=75\\%"},{"k":"p","text":"The notation changes, but the quantity does not. This week we use all of these forms and move freely between them."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Adding and subtracting in real contexts","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Parts can only be added when they are the same size, so first rewrite the fractions over a common denominator (best of all, the LCM of the denominators). For example, $\\text{LCM}(12,18)=36$, so"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{5}{12}+\\frac{7}{18}=\\frac{15}{36}+\\frac{14}{36}=\\frac{29}{36}"},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Mixed numbers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Change mixed numbers into improper fractions before you add or subtract. This avoids mistakes with “borrowing”:"},{"k":"math","tex":"3\\frac{1}{4}-1\\frac{5}{8}=\\frac{13}{4}-\\frac{13}{8}=\\frac{26}{8}-\\frac{13}{8}=\\frac{13}{8}=1\\frac{5}{8}"}]},{"k":"p","text":"In questions with several steps, follow the order of operations: **B**rackets first, then **O**f, **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication, then **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction (BODMAS), working from left to right. Always give the units in the final answer."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Multiplying, dividing and fractions of quantities","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Multiplying fractions finds a part of a part:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{2}{5}\\times\\frac{3}{4}=\\frac{6}{20}=\\frac{3}{10}"},{"k":"p","text":"To find a fraction **of a quantity**, multiply: $\\dfrac{3}{8}$ of GH₵240 is $\\dfrac{3}{8}\\times240=3\\times30=$ GH₵90."},{"k":"p","text":"To divide by a fraction, multiply by the **reciprocal** of the divisor:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{7}{12}\\div\\frac{14}{15}=\\frac{7}{12}\\times\\frac{15}{14}=\\frac{5}{8}"},{"k":"p","text":"Dividing answers the question “how many of these fit into that?”. For example, $\\dfrac{9}{10}$ kg of seed fills $\\dfrac{9}{10}\\div\\dfrac{3}{40}=12$ bags of $\\dfrac{3}{40}$ kg."},{"k":"fig","id":"w05-bags","caption":"$\\frac{9}{10}$ kg is $\\frac{36}{40}$ kg, which makes 12 groups of $\\frac{3}{40}$ kg."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Cancel factors, not terms","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Cancel common **factors** before multiplying to keep the numbers small: $\\dfrac{7}{12}\\times\\dfrac{15}{14}=\\dfrac{1\\times5}{4\\times2}$ after cancelling $7$ and $3$. You may **not** cancel part of a sum: in $\\dfrac{2+3}{5}$ you cannot cancel the $2$ or the $3$ with the $5$."}]}],"figs":["w05-bags"]},{"title":"Decimals and place value","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Each place to the right of the decimal point is one tenth of the place before it: tenths, hundredths, thousandths, and so on."},{"k":"fig","id":"w05-placevalue","caption":"$3.407=3+\\frac{4}{10}+\\frac{0}{100}+\\frac{7}{1000}$. Moving one place to the right divides the place value by 10."},{"k":"p","text":"The zero in $3.407$ is a **placeholder**: without it the number would be $3.47$, a different number. Zeros at the **end** of a decimal do not change its value: $0.6=0.60=0.600$."},{"k":"p","text":"To change a terminating decimal into a fraction, use the place value of the last digit as the denominator, then simplify:"},{"k":"math","tex":"0.625=\\frac{625}{1000}=\\frac{5}{8}"}],"figs":["w05-placevalue"]},{"title":"Recurring decimals","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To change a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. If a remainder appears for the second time, the digits from then on repeat for ever."},{"k":"fig","id":"w05-longdiv","caption":"In $5\\div6$ the remainder 2 keeps coming back, so $\\frac{5}{6}=0.8333\\ldots=0.8\\dot{3}$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Dot notation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A dot over a digit shows that it repeats: $0.8\\dot{3}=0.8333\\ldots$ Dots over the first and last digits of a block show that the whole block repeats: $0.\\dot{2}\\dot{7}=0.272727\\ldots$ and $0.\\dot{1}2\\dot{3}=0.123123\\ldots$"}]},{"k":"p","text":"**Changing a recurring decimal into a fraction.** Let $x=0.272727\\ldots$ The repeating block has 2 digits, so multiply by $10^2=100$ and subtract to remove the repeating part:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\begin{aligned}100x&=27.2727\\ldots\\\\x&=\\phantom{2}0.2727\\ldots\\\\99x&=27\\end{aligned}"},{"k":"p","text":"So $x=\\dfrac{27}{99}=\\dfrac{3}{11}$. This is a proof, not a guess."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"When only part of the decimal repeats","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $x=0.8\\dot{3}$, first move the non-repeating digit: $10x=8.333\\ldots$ and $100x=83.333\\ldots$ Subtracting gives $90x=75$, so $x=\\dfrac{75}{90}=\\dfrac{5}{6}$."}]}],"figs":["w05-longdiv"]},{"title":"Additive inverses","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **additive inverse** of a number is the number you add to it to get $0$. The additive inverse of $a$ is $-a$."},{"k":"ul","items":["The additive inverse of $\\dfrac{7}{9}$ is $-\\dfrac{7}{9}$, because $\\dfrac{7}{9}+\\left(-\\dfrac{7}{9}\\right)=0$.","The additive inverse of $-\\dfrac{11}{6}$ is $\\dfrac{11}{6}$.","$0$ is its own additive inverse."]},{"k":"p","text":"On a number line, $a$ and $-a$ are the same distance from $0$ on opposite sides."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Multiplicative inverses (reciprocals)","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **multiplicative inverse** (reciprocal) of a non-zero number is the number you multiply it by to get $1$. The reciprocal of $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ is $\\dfrac{b}{a}$, and it keeps the same sign."},{"k":"ul","items":["The reciprocal of $\\dfrac{7}{12}$ is $\\dfrac{12}{7}$, because $\\dfrac{7}{12}\\times\\dfrac{12}{7}=1$.","The reciprocal of $-\\dfrac{3}{10}$ is $-\\dfrac{10}{3}$.","The reciprocal of a whole number $5$ is $\\dfrac{1}{5}$."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w05-inverses","caption":"For $\\frac{4}{5}$: the additive inverse $-\\frac{4}{5}$ is its mirror image in 0, and the multiplicative inverse $\\frac{5}{4}$ makes a rectangle of area 1."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Zero has no reciprocal","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"There is no number $b$ with $0\\times b=1$, because $0\\times b$ is always $0$. So $0$ has an additive inverse (itself) but **no** multiplicative inverse."}]},{"k":"table","head":["Number","Additive inverse (sum $=0$)","Multiplicative inverse (product $=1$)"],"rows":[["$\\dfrac{4}{5}$","$-\\dfrac{4}{5}$","$\\dfrac{5}{4}$"],["$-\\dfrac{3}{8}$","$\\dfrac{3}{8}$","$-\\dfrac{8}{3}$"],["$2.5$","$-2.5$","$\\dfrac{2}{5}=0.4$"],["$0$","$0$","none"]]}],"figs":["w05-inverses"]},{"title":"Fractions, decimals and percentages","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **percentage** is a number of parts per hundred. To move between the three forms:"},{"k":"ul","items":["fraction $\\to$ decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator;","decimal $\\to$ percentage: multiply by $100\\%$;","percentage $\\to$ fraction: write over $100$ and simplify."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w05-fdp","caption":"$\\frac{7}{20}=0.35=35\\%$: thirty-five squares out of one hundred."},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $62.5\\%=0.625=\\dfrac{625}{1000}=\\dfrac{5}{8}$. Writing an answer in a second form is a good way to check that it is reasonable."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Where you meet this","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Shop discounts are given as percentages, fuel prices as decimals of a cedi, and recipes and measuring cups use fractions. A trader who knows that $\\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25=25\\%$ can switch between them instantly."}]}],"figs":["w05-fdp"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Adding mixed numbers","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A water tank contains $2\\dfrac{3}{4}$ litres. What fraction of the sack remains?"}],"steps":["Let the whole sack be $1$.","$\\text{LCM}(6,20)=60$. Used: $\\dfrac{50}{60}+\\dfrac{9}{60}=\\dfrac{59}{60}$.","Remaining: $1-\\dfrac{59}{60}=\\dfrac{1}{60}$.","The answer is positive and small, which makes sense: almost all the rice was used."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{1}{60}$ of the sack","figs":[]},{"title":"Packing seeds","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school is given $\\dfrac{9}{10}$ kg of seeds and packs them into bags of $\\dfrac{3}{40}$ kg each. What is the place value of the final digit $5$?"}],"steps":["There are four decimal places, so $0.0875=\\dfrac{875}{10000}$.","$875=5^3\\times7$ and $10000=2^4\\times5^4$, so $\\text{HCF}=5^3=125$.","$\\dfrac{875\\div125}{10000\\div125}=\\dfrac{7}{80}$.","The $5$ is in the fourth decimal place, the ten-thousandths place, so it is worth $\\dfrac{5}{10000}$."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{7}{80}$; the $5$ is five ten-thousandths.","figs":[]},{"title":"A recurring decimal is rational","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Without a calculator, show that $0.\\dot{1}\\dot{8}=0.181818\\ldots$ is rational, and write it as a fraction in its lowest terms."}],"steps":["Let $x=0.181818\\ldots$ The block $18$ has two digits.","Multiply by $100$: $100x=18.181818\\ldots$","Subtract: $100x-x=18$, so $99x=18$.","$x=\\dfrac{18}{99}=\\dfrac{2}{11}$.","It is a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator, so it is rational."],"answer":"$0.\\dot{1}\\dot{8}=\\dfrac{2}{11}$","figs":[]},{"title":"Both inverses","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For $a=-\\dfrac{7}{12}$, find the additive inverse and the multiplicative inverse. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w06">{"year":1,"week":6,"id":"y1w06","title":"Connecting Fractions, Decimals and Percentages","subtitle":"One number in three forms; hundred squares and benchmark values; accurate conversion; rounding and estimation; percentages of amounts and finding the whole.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["Write the same quantity as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and show it with a model.","Convert accurately between the three forms, including percentages above 100%.","Round decimals and percentages correctly and use benchmarks to check answers.","Find a percentage of an amount, and find the whole when a part is known.","Solve real-life problems on shares, marks, budgets and comparisons."],"keywords":["fraction","decimal","percentage","hundred square","benchmark","decimal places","rounding","percentage of an amount","percentage points"],"notes":[{"title":"One quantity, three forms","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Fractions, decimals and percentages are not three separate topics. They are three ways of writing **the same number**:"},{"k":"ul","items":["a **fraction** shows the part–whole relationship, e.g. $\\dfrac{3}{8}$;","a **decimal** shows base-ten place value, e.g. $0.375$;","a **percentage** shows the amount per hundred, e.g. $37.5\\%$."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w06-three","caption":"Each eighth lines up with a decimal and a percentage. The highlighted column shows $\\frac{3}{8}=0.375=37.5\\%$."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Changing between the forms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Fraction $\\to$ decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator.","Decimal $\\to$ percentage: multiply by $100\\%$.","Percentage $\\to$ fraction: write the number over $100$ and simplify.","Percentage $\\to$ decimal: divide by $100$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"These are changes of **form**, not changes of amount."}],"figs":["w06-three"]},{"title":"Hundred squares and benchmark values","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A hundred square has 100 equal small squares, so each square is $1\\%$ of the whole. Shading 25 squares shows $\\dfrac{25}{100}=\\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25=25\\%$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w06-hundred","caption":"Left: 25 of 100 squares is one quarter. Right: the grid in five equal groups of 20; three groups make $\\frac{3}{5}=60\\%$."},{"k":"p","text":"Learn these **benchmarks** by their meaning, not just their symbols. They make estimation quick and reliable."},{"k":"table","head":["Fraction","Decimal","Percentage"],"rows":[["$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$0.5$","$50\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{4}$","$0.25$","$25\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{3}{4}$","$0.75$","$75\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{5}$","$0.2$","$20\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{10}$","$0.1$","$10\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{8}$","$0.125$","$12.5\\%$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{3}$","$0.\\dot{3}$","$33\\dfrac{1}{3}\\%$"]]}],"figs":["w06-hundred"]},{"title":"Decimals to fractions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For a decimal with $n$ digits after the point, write the digits (without the point) over $10^n$, then simplify:"},{"k":"math","tex":"0.0375=\\frac{375}{10000}=\\frac{3}{80}\\qquad\\qquad1.125=\\frac{1125}{1000}=\\frac{9}{8}=1\\frac{1}{8}"},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Zeros in decimals","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Zeros at the **end** do not change the value: $0.4=0.40=0.400$.","Zeros straight **after the point** do change it: $0.04$ is ten times smaller than $0.4$, because the $4$ has moved from the tenths place to the hundredths place."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Fractions and percentages","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To write $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ as a percentage, multiply by $100\\%$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{7}{16}\\times100\\%=\\frac{700}{16}\\%=43.75\\%"},{"k":"p","text":"Notice that $0.4375$ is the decimal and $43.75\\%$ is the percentage. Only write the $\\%$ sign on a percentage."},{"k":"p","text":"A percentage can be **more than** $100\\%$ when the amount is larger than the whole: $\\dfrac{9}{8}=1.125=112.5\\%$."},{"k":"p","text":"To change a percentage into a fraction, divide by $100$ and simplify: $62.5\\%=0.625=\\dfrac{625}{1000}=\\dfrac{5}{8}$. If the percentage itself contains a fraction, deal with that first:"},{"k":"math","tex":"33\\frac{1}{3}\\%=\\frac{100}{3}\\%=\\frac{100}{3}\\times\\frac{1}{100}=\\frac{1}{3}"}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Rounding and estimation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To round $0.37684$ to three decimal places, keep $0.376$ and look at the **next** digit, $8$. Since it is $5$ or more, round up to $0.377$, which is about $37.7\\%$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w06-rounding","caption":"$0.37684$ lies past the halfway point $0.3765$, so it is nearer to $0.377$."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Round only at the end","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Rounding in the middle of a calculation adds small errors that can grow. Keep exact values (or extra decimal places) until the final answer, then round as the question asks."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Use benchmarks to check answers. $\\dfrac{7}{15}$ is a little less than $\\dfrac{1}{2}$, so it must be a little less than $50\\%$; an answer of $4.7\\%$ or $470\\%$ is clearly wrong. (In fact $\\dfrac{7}{15}=46.\\dot{6}\\%$.)"}],"figs":["w06-rounding"]},{"title":"Percentage of an amount, and finding the whole","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Percentage of an amount.** Change the percentage into a fraction or decimal and multiply:"},{"k":"math","tex":"35\\%\\text{ of }240=\\frac{35}{100}\\times240=84"},{"k":"p","text":"So $35\\%$ of GH₵240 is GH₵84."},{"k":"p","text":"**Finding the whole.** If GH₵84 is $35\\%$ of a total, then $1\\%$ is $84\\div35=2.40$, so $100\\%$ is GH₵240. In one step: total $=84\\div0.35=$ GH₵240."},{"k":"fig","id":"w06-whole","caption":"The bar is the whole (100%). Knowing that 35% is GH₵84 lets us find 1% and then 100%."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Ask: which quantity is missing?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Every percentage problem links three things: the **percentage**, the **part** and the **whole**."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{part}=\\text{percentage}\\times\\text{whole}"},{"k":"p","text":"Decide which one the question asks for before you calculate."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w06-budget","caption":"A budget of GH₵1,280: $37.5\\%=\\frac{3}{8}$ goes to food and the remaining $62.5\\%=\\frac{5}{8}$ to other needs (Worked Example 6.4)."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Percentage points","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If an estimate of $45\\%$ should have been $43.75\\%$, the error is $45-43.75=1.25$ **percentage points**. Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages; they are not the same as a percentage change."}]}],"figs":["w06-whole","w06-budget"]},{"title":"Inverses in every form","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Inverses work the same way whatever the form. For $\\dfrac{3}{8}=0.375=37.5\\%$:"},{"k":"ul","items":["the **additive inverse** is $-\\dfrac{3}{8}=-0.375$, because the sum is $0$;","the **reciprocal** is $\\dfrac{8}{3}$, because $\\dfrac{3}{8}\\times\\dfrac{8}{3}=1=100\\%$."]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"A strategy for harder problems","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["Identify the whole.","Choose the most useful form (fraction, decimal or percentage).","Work without unnecessary rounding.","Convert back to the form and units the question asks for, and check that the answer is reasonable."]}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"One share in three forms","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A community library owns 640 textbooks, of which 248 are mathematics textbooks. Since $\\text{HCF}(248,640)=8$, this is $\\dfrac{31}{80}$.","Decimal: $31\\div80=0.3875$.","Percentage: $0.3875\\times100\\%=38.75\\%$.","Check: $0.3875\\times640=248$ ✓."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{31}{80}=0.3875=38.75\\%$","figs":[]},{"title":"How full is the tank?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A tank is $62.5\\%$ full. Write the full part as a fraction in its lowest terms. If the capacity is 360 litres, how much water is in the tank?"}],"steps":["$62.5\\%=0.625=\\dfrac{625}{1000}=\\dfrac{5}{8}$.","$\\dfrac{5}{8}$ of $360$: $360\\div8=45$ and $45\\times5=225$ litres.","Check: $225\\div360=0.625=62.5\\%$ ✓."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{5}{8}$ of the tank, which is 225 litres.","figs":[]},{"title":"Marks as a percentage","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner scores 47 marks out of 64. Is it more than $70\\%$?"}],"steps":["Fraction: $\\dfrac{47}{64}$.","Percentage: $\\dfrac{47}{64}\\times100\\%=73.4375\\%$.","To 2 decimal places, look at the third decimal digit, $7$: round up to $73.44\\%$.","$73.44\\%-70\\%=3.44$ percentage points."],"answer":"$73.44\\%$, which is more than $70\\%$.","figs":[]},{"title":"A family budget","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A family budgets GH₵1,280 a month. Food gets $37.5\\%$ of the budget. Find the amount for food, and the fraction of the budget left for other things."}],"steps":["$37.5\\%=\\dfrac{3}{8}$.","Food: $\\dfrac{3}{8}\\times1280=3\\times160=$ GH₵480.","Left: $100\\%-37.5\\%=62.5\\%=\\dfrac{5}{8}$.","Check: $480+\\dfrac{5}{8}\\times1280=480+800=1280$ ✓."],"answer":"Food: GH₵480; the remaining share is $\\dfrac{5}{8}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"An exact recurring percentage","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write $0.666\\ldots$ as a fraction, then as an exact percentage."}],"steps":["Let $x=0.666\\ldots$; then $10x=6.666\\ldots$","Subtract: $9x=6$, so $x=\\dfrac{6}{9}=\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","Percentage: $\\dfrac{2}{3}\\times100\\%=\\dfrac{200}{3}\\%=66\\dfrac{2}{3}\\%$.","$66.67\\%$ is only a rounded value; $66\\dfrac{2}{3}\\%$ is exact."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{2}{3}=66\\dfrac{2}{3}\\%$ exactly.","figs":[]},{"title":"Finding the whole school","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$18\\%$ of the learners in a school travel by bicycle. If 126 learners travel by bicycle, how many learners are in the school?"}],"steps":["Let the number of learners be $N$. Then $0.18N=126$.","$N=126\\div0.18=\\dfrac{12600}{18}=700$.","Check: $18\\%$ of $700=0.18\\times700=126$ ✓."],"answer":"700 learners","figs":[]},{"title":"Error in percentage points","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A shopkeeper says that $\\dfrac{7}{16}$ is about $45\\%$. Find the exact percentage and the error in percentage points."}],"steps":["$\\dfrac{7}{16}=7\\div16=0.4375=43.75\\%$.","Error: $45-43.75=1.25$ percentage points.","The estimate is too high by $1.25$ percentage points."],"answer":"Exact value $43.75\\%$; error $1.25$ percentage points.","figs":[]},{"title":"More than 100 percent","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer expected to harvest 160 bags of maize but harvested 200 bags. Express the harvest as a percentage of the expected amount."}],"steps":["Fraction of the expected amount: $\\dfrac{200}{160}=\\dfrac{5}{4}$.","Percentage: $\\dfrac{5}{4}\\times100\\%=125\\%$.","It is more than $100\\%$ because the harvest was larger than the whole that was expected."],"answer":"$125\\%$ of the expected harvest","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 6","items":["Fraction $\\xrightarrow{\\ \\div\\ }$ decimal $\\xrightarrow{\\times100\\%}$ percentage, and back again.","Decimal with $n$ decimal places $=\\dfrac{\\text{digits}}{10^n}$, then simplify.","Percentage of an amount: $\\text{part}=\\dfrac{p}{100}\\times\\text{whole}$.","Finding the whole: $\\text{whole}=\\text{part}\\div\\dfrac{p}{100}$.","Round only at the end; check with benchmarks such as $\\dfrac{1}{2}=50\\%$ and $\\dfrac{1}{4}=25\\%$."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Express $\\dfrac{7}{20}$ as a percentage.","options":["$28\\%$","$35\\%$","$14\\%$","$70\\%$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$\\dfrac{7}{20}=\\dfrac{35}{100}=0.35=35\\%$."},{"q":"Convert $0.875$ into a fraction in its lowest terms.","options":["$\\dfrac{5}{6}$","$\\dfrac{7}{8}$","$\\dfrac{9}{10}$","$\\dfrac{3}{4}$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$0.875=\\dfrac{875}{1000}=\\dfrac{7}{8}$."},{"q":"Write $62.5\\%$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.","options":["$\\dfrac{2}{3}$","$\\dfrac{3}{4}$","$\\dfrac{5}{8}$","$\\dfrac{7}{12}$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$62.5\\%=0.625=\\dfrac{625}{1000}=\\dfrac{5}{8}$."},{"q":"A class has 45 learners and 18 are girls. What percentage are girls?","options":["$45\\%$","$35\\%$","$50\\%$","$40\\%$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$\\dfrac{18}{45}=\\dfrac{2}{5}=0.4=40\\%$."},{"q":"What is $12.5\\%$ of $320$?","options":["$32$","$36$","$40$","$48$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$12.5\\%=\\dfrac{1}{8}$, and $320\\div8=40$."},{"q":"A learner scores 36 out of 48. What is the percentage score?","options":["$70\\%$","$75\\%$","$80\\%$","$72\\%$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$\\dfrac{36}{48}=\\dfrac{3}{4}=75\\%$."},{"q":"Which fraction in its lowest terms is equal to $0.045$?","options":["$\\dfrac{9}{100}$","$\\dfrac{1}{25}$","$\\dfrac{9}{200}$","$\\dfrac{3}{20}$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$0.045=\\dfrac{45}{1000}=\\dfrac{9}{200}$."},{"q":"If 24 is $30\\%$ of a number, what is the number?","options":["$72$","$60$","$90$","$80$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$0.3N=24$, so $N=24\\div0.3=80$."},{"q":"Rounded to 2 decimal places, $0.3769$ is","options":["$0.37$","$0.377$","$0.40$","$0.38$"],"correct":3,"explain":"The third decimal digit is $6$, which is $5$ or more, so $0.37$ rounds up to $0.38$."},{"q":"Which fraction is exactly equal to $150\\%$?","options":["$\\dfrac{3}{4}$","$\\dfrac{3}{2}$","$\\dfrac{5}{4}$","$\\dfrac{2}{3}$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$150\\%=\\dfrac{150}{100}=\\dfrac{3}{2}=1.5$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Write $0.0075$ as a fraction in its lowest terms and as a percentage.","a":"$\\dfrac{75}{10000}=\\dfrac{3}{400}$; $0.75\\%$."},{"q":"A school spends $42.5\\%$ of GH₵8,400 on supplies. How much is spent, and what fraction of the money remains?","a":"$0.425\\times8400=$ GH₵3,570; remaining $57.5\\%=\\dfrac{23}{40}$."},{"q":"A learner is told that 21 marks are $37.5\\%$ of the total. What is the total number of marks?","a":"$21\\div0.375=56$ marks."},{"q":"Write $\\dfrac{11}{24}$ as a percentage correct to two decimal places, showing the rounding.","a":"$\\dfrac{11}{24}=0.458333\\ldots=45.8333\\ldots\\%$; the third decimal digit is $3$, so it rounds to $45.83\\%$."},{"q":"Three groups receive $12.5\\%$, $37.5\\%$ and $\\dfrac{1}{4}$ of a grant. What percentage is left?","a":"$12.5+37.5+25=75\\%$ is given out, so $25\\%$ is left."},{"q":"Write $1.125$ as an improper fraction, a mixed number and a percentage.","a":"$\\dfrac{9}{8}=1\\dfrac{1}{8}=112.5\\%$"},{"q":"Ama scored $\\dfrac{17}{25}$ in Test 1 and $\\dfrac{26}{40}$ in Test 2. Use percentages to decide in which test she did better.","a":"Test 1: $68\\%$; Test 2: $65\\%$. She did better in Test 1."},{"q":"Round $0.48627$ to (a) 2 decimal places (b) 3 decimal places, and write each as a percentage.","a":"(a) $0.49=49\\%$ (b) $0.486=48.6\\%$"}],"theory":[{"q":"Use a hundred square to explain why $\\dfrac{3}{5}=60\\%$.","steps":["Split the 100 squares into 5 equal groups; each group has $100\\div5=20$ squares.","Shade 3 groups: $3\\times20=60$ squares.","$60$ squares out of $100$ is $\\dfrac{60}{100}=60\\%$."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{3}{5}=\\dfrac{60}{100}=60\\%$","model":null},{"q":"A farmer harvested 840 crates of produce, and $17.5\\%$ were tomatoes. How many crates of tomatoes were harvested?","steps":["$17.5\\%=0.175=\\dfrac{175}{1000}=\\dfrac{7}{40}$.","$\\dfrac{7}{40}\\times840=7\\times21=147$."],"answer":"147 crates of tomatoes","model":null},{"q":"Explain why $0.08$ and $0.8$ are different numbers, even though both contain only the digit $8$.","steps":["In $0.8$ the $8$ is in the tenths place: $0.8=\\dfrac{8}{10}$.","In $0.08$ the $8$ is in the hundredths place: $0.08=\\dfrac{8}{100}$.","One tenth is ten hundredths, so $0.8$ is ten times $0.08$."],"answer":"The place of the digit gives its value: $0.8=10\\times0.08$.","model":null},{"q":"Use algebra to write $0.\\dot{3}\\dot{6}=0.363636\\ldots$ as a fraction.","steps":["Let $x=0.363636\\ldots$","Then $100x=36.363636\\ldots$","Subtract: $99x=36$, so $x=\\dfrac{36}{99}=\\dfrac{4}{11}$."],"answer":"$0.\\dot{3}\\dot{6}=\\dfrac{4}{11}$","model":null},{"q":"A company gives $\\dfrac{5}{16}$ of its funds to transport. Write this share as a percentage, and the remaining share as a decimal and a percentage.","steps":["$\\dfrac{5}{16}=5\\div16=0.3125=31.25\\%$.","Remaining: $1-\\dfrac{5}{16}=\\dfrac{11}{16}$.","$\\dfrac{11}{16}=0.6875=68.75\\%$.","Check: $31.25\\%+68.75\\%=100\\%$ ✓."],"answer":"Transport $31.25\\%$; remaining $0.6875=68.75\\%$.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can write the same number as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.","I can use a hundred square and benchmark values to estimate.","I can convert decimals with many places, and percentages above 100%.","I can round correctly and I round only at the end.","I can find a percentage of an amount and find the whole from a part.","I can explain the difference between percent and percentage points."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[1]},{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[2]}],[{"j":5,"notes":true,"exs":[3,4,5,6,7]},{"j":6,"notes":true,"exs":[]}]],"exSec":[0,3,4,5,5,5,5,5],"quizSec":[5,3,3,5,5,5,3,5,4,3],"exerSec":[3,3,5,4,0,3,3,4],"thSec":[1,0,2,3,5],"sumSec":[5,2,5,5,1],"chkSec":[2,1,3,4,5,5],"weights":[1597.65,807.05,569.1500000000001,1148.35,1559.7,4930,589.5],"figs":[{"id":"w06-three","sec":0,"lesson":1,"caption":"Each eighth lines up with a decimal and a percentage. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w07">{"year":1,"week":7,"id":"y1w07","title":"Applications of Percentages in Household Finance","subtitle":"Percentage increase and decrease, multipliers, discounts, reverse percentages, profit and loss, commission, tax and household budgets.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["Calculate percentage increase, percentage decrease and discounts from the correct original amount.","Use multipliers, and solve reverse-percentage problems to find an original price.","Calculate profit, loss, commission and tax in household and business contexts.","Explain why successive percentage changes are multiplied, not added.","Compare offers and budgets and interpret the answers in context."],"keywords":["percentage change","multiplier","discount","marked price","selling price","cost price","profit","loss","commission","tax","reverse percentage"],"notes":[{"title":"Percentages in money problems","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A percentage means “parts in every hundred”. So $15\\%$ means 15 out of every 100, not GH₵15 (unless the original amount is GH₵100). In every money question, first identify the **original amount**, the base on which the percentage is taken."},{"k":"p","text":"There are three different tasks:"},{"k":"ol","items":["finding a percentage **of** a known amount;","finding what percentage one amount is **of another**;","finding the **original** amount when the changed amount is known."]},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Percentage change","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{percentage change}=\\frac{\\text{change}}{\\text{original}}\\times100\\%"},{"k":"p","text":"For an increase the change is $\\text{new}-\\text{original}$; for a decrease it is $\\text{original}-\\text{new}$."}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Always divide by the original","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The most common examination error is dividing by the **new** amount. If a price rises from GH₵450 to GH₵540, the increase is $\\dfrac{90}{450}\\times100\\%=20\\%$, not $\\dfrac{90}{540}\\times100\\%$."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Multipliers: the quickest reliable method","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The original amount is $100\\%$, which is a multiplier of $1$."},{"k":"ul","items":["A $12\\%$ **increase** gives $100\\%+12\\%=112\\%$ of the original, so multiply by $1.12$.","A $12\\%$ **decrease** gives $100\\%-12\\%=88\\%$ of the original, so multiply by $0.88$."]},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Multipliers","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Increase by $r\\%$: $\\;\\text{new}=\\text{original}\\times\\left(1+\\dfrac{r}{100}\\right)$","Decrease by $r\\%$: $\\;\\text{new}=\\text{original}\\times\\left(1-\\dfrac{r}{100}\\right)$","Reverse: $\\;\\text{original}=\\text{new}\\div\\text{multiplier}$"]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w07-multiplier","caption":"To undo a percentage change, divide by the same multiplier. Adding 15% back to the reduced price does not give the original."},{"k":"p","text":"For example, a price of GH₵896 after a $20\\%$ reduction is $80\\%$ of the original, so the original is $896\\div0.80=$ GH₵1,120, **not** $896\\times1.20$."}],"figs":["w07-multiplier"]},{"title":"Discount, marked price and selling price","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **marked price** is the price on the tag before any reduction.","The **discount** is the amount taken off: $\\text{discount}=\\text{rate}\\times\\text{marked price}$.","The **selling price** is what the customer pays: $\\text{marked price}-\\text{discount}$."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w07-discount","caption":"After a 20% discount the customer pays 80% of the marked price. The part paid and the discount together make 100%."},{"k":"p","text":"**Successive discounts** are applied one after the other, each to the price at that moment. A $20\\%$ discount followed by a $10\\%$ discount gives a combined multiplier of $0.80\\times0.90=0.72$: a total reduction of $28\\%$, not $30\\%$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w07-successive","caption":"The second discount is 10% of GH₵1,200, not of GH₵1,500, so the total discount is 28%."},{"k":"box","kind":"note","title":"Order matters","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A fixed GH₵30 coupon used after a $15\\%$ discount is not the same as a further $15\\%$ off. Follow the order given in the question and write down each intermediate amount."}]}],"figs":["w07-discount","w07-successive"]},{"title":"Profit and loss","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **cost price** (CP) is the total cost of buying an item and getting it ready for sale, including transport, repairs or packaging when these are given. The **selling price** (SP) is what the buyer pays."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Profit and loss","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Profit $=\\text{SP}-\\text{CP}$ (when SP is greater than CP)","Loss $=\\text{CP}-\\text{SP}$ (when SP is less than CP)","$\\text{Profit }\\%=\\dfrac{\\text{profit}}{\\text{CP}}\\times100\\%$ and $\\text{Loss }\\%=\\dfrac{\\text{loss}}{\\text{CP}}\\times100\\%$"]}]},{"k":"p","text":"Profit and loss percentages are worked out on the **cost price**. A trader who buys for GH₵400 and sells for GH₵500 makes GH₵100 profit, which is $25\\%$ of the cost price, even though it is only $20\\%$ of the selling price."},{"k":"fig","id":"w07-profit","caption":"The same GH₵100 profit is 25% of the cost price but 20% of the selling price. Profit percentage always uses the cost price."},{"k":"p","text":"For a $15\\%$ profit, $\\text{SP}=1.15\\times\\text{CP}$; for a $15\\%$ loss, $\\text{SP}=0.85\\times\\text{CP}$. To find the cost price from the selling price, divide by the multiplier."}],"figs":["w07-profit"]},{"title":"Commission, tax and bills","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Commission** is payment for making sales: $\\text{commission}=\\text{rate}\\times\\text{qualifying sales}$. A salesperson may get a fixed salary **plus** commission; work out the two parts separately and add them."},{"k":"p","text":"**Tax** is calculated on a stated amount (the tax base). If a $10\\%$ tax is added after a discount, find the discounted price first, then add $10\\%$ of that amount."},{"k":"box","kind":"note","title":"About the tax rates","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The tax rates in this lesson are examples given in each question. They are not a statement of Ghana’s current tax rules."}]},{"k":"p","text":"**Household bills** often have a fixed charge plus a charge for each unit used. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w08">{"year":1,"week":8,"id":"y1w08","title":"Simple and Compound Interest and Financial Growth","subtitle":"Principal, rate, time and amount; simple interest and its reverse problems; compound interest with annual, half-yearly and quarterly compounding; depreciation and growth factors.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["Explain principal, rate, time, interest, amount and compounding period.","Use the simple-interest formula, and rearrange it to find the principal, rate or time.","Calculate compound interest year by year and with the formula, including half-yearly and quarterly compounding.","Use growth and decay factors for depreciation and successive percentage changes.","Compare savings and loan options and interpret the results."],"keywords":["principal","interest rate","simple interest","compound interest","amount","compounding period","growth factor","depreciation","effective rate"],"notes":[{"title":"The meaning of interest","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"When you borrow money you usually pay an extra charge called **interest**; when you save or invest money you may **earn** interest."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Key terms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Principal** $P$: the money first saved or borrowed.","**Rate** $r\\%$: the percentage charged or earned per stated period, usually per year (per annum, p.a.).","**Time** $t$: how long the money is saved or borrowed, in the same unit as the rate.","**Interest** $I$: the extra money earned or paid.","**Amount** $A$: the total at the end, $A=P+I$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"If the rate is per year, the time must be in years. For example, $9$ months $=\\dfrac{9}{12}=0.75$ year and $30$ months $=\\dfrac{30}{12}=2.5$ years."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Read the question","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The question must say whether the interest is **simple** or **compound**. Interest begins to earn interest."},{"k":"p","text":"GH₵1,000 at $10\\%$ compound interest becomes GH₵1,100 after one year and $1100\\times1.10=$ GH₵1,210 after two years. The second year earns GH₵110, not GH₵100."},{"k":"fig","id":"w08-stack","caption":"Simple interest adds the same GH₵100 each year. Compound interest adds 10% of the current balance, so it adds more every year."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Compound interest (once a year)","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"A=P\\left(1+\\frac{r}{100}\\right)^{n}\\qquad\\qquad\\text{compound interest}=A-P"},{"k":"p","text":"$n$ is the number of years."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w08-growth","caption":"Over 10 years, simple interest grows in a straight line but compound interest curves upwards."}],"figs":["w08-stack","w08-growth"]},{"title":"Compounding more than once a year","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Banks often compound half-yearly, quarterly or monthly. Here $r\\%$ is the nominal annual rate and $t$ is in years."}]},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $12\\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly for 18 months gives a rate of $12\\%\\div4=3\\%$ per quarter for $4\\times1.5=6$ quarters."},{"k":"fig","id":"w08-quarters","caption":"Eighteen months is 6 quarters. Find the annual rate."}],"steps":["$t=\\dfrac{30}{12}=2.5$ years.","$r=\\dfrac{100I}{Pt}=\\dfrac{100\\times720}{4000\\times2.5}=\\dfrac{72000}{10000}=7.2$.","Check: $\\dfrac{4000\\times7.2\\times2.5}{100}=720$ ✓."],"answer":"$7.2\\%$ per annum","figs":[]},{"title":"Half-yearly compounding","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"GH₵6,000 earns $6\\%$ per annum compounded half-yearly for 2 years. Find the amount and the interest, correct to 2 decimal places."}],"steps":["Rate per half-year: $6\\%\\div2=3\\%$, so the factor is $1.03$.","Number of half-years: $2\\times2=4$.","$A=6000\\times1.03^4=6000\\times1.12550881=6753.05$ (2 d.p.).","Interest: $6753.05-6000=753.05$."],"answer":"Amount GH₵6,753.05; interest GH₵753.05.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 8","items":["Simple interest: $I=\\dfrac{Prt}{100}$ and $A=P+I$.","Rearranged: $P=\\dfrac{100I}{rt}$, $r=\\dfrac{100I}{Pt}$, $t=\\dfrac{100I}{Pr}$.","Compound interest: $A=P\\left(1+\\dfrac{r}{100}\\right)^n$; interest $=A-P$.","Compounding $m$ times a year: $A=P\\left(1+\\dfrac{r}{100m}\\right)^{mt}$.","Depreciation at $r\\%$ a year: $V=P\\left(1-\\dfrac{r}{100}\\right)^t$."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"What simple interest is earned on GH₵3,000 at $8\\%$ per annum for 9 months?","options":["GH₵120","GH₵180","GH₵240","GH₵270"],"correct":1,"explain":"$t=\\dfrac{9}{12}=0.75$ year, so $I=3000\\times0.08\\times0.75=180$."},{"q":"Which expression gives the amount on GH₵2,000 invested for 3 years at $5\\%$ compounded annually?","options":["$2000(1.15)^3$","$2000(0.95)^3$","$2000(1.05)^3$","$2000(1.05\\times3)$"],"correct":2,"explain":"The growth factor $1.05$ is applied once for each of the 3 years."},{"q":"A GH₵5,000 loan costs GH₵750 simple interest over 3 years. Estimate the population after 3 years.","a":"$50000\\times1.04^3=56243.2$, so about 56,243 people."},{"q":"On GH₵1,000 for 3 years, which is better for a saver: $9\\%$ simple interest or $8\\%$ compound interest (annually)?","a":"Simple: GH₵1,270. Compound: $1000\\times1.08^3=$ GH₵1,259.71. The $9\\%$ simple interest is better here."},{"q":"Find the effective annual rate of $6\\%$ per annum compounded quarterly, to 2 decimal places.","a":"$1.015^4=1.06136\\ldots$, so about $6.14\\%$."}],"theory":[{"q":"GH₵7,200 is invested at $5.5\\%$ simple interest for 20 months. Find the interest and the amount.","steps":["$t=\\dfrac{20}{12}=\\dfrac{5}{3}$ years.","$I=7200\\times0.055\\times\\dfrac{5}{3}=396\\times\\dfrac{5}{3}=660$.","$A=7200+660=7860$."],"answer":"Interest GH₵660; amount GH₵7,860.","model":null},{"q":"An amount of GH₵6,655 is due after 3 years at $10\\%$ compound interest per annum. Find the money first invested.","steps":["$A=P\\times1.1^3$, so $6655=1.331P$.","$P=6655\\div1.331=5000$.","Check: $5000\\to5500\\to6050\\to6655$ ✓."],"answer":"GH₵5,000","model":null},{"q":"A student saves GH₵9,000 for 2 years at $8\\%$ per annum. Compare simple interest with annual compound interest.","steps":["Simple: $I=9000\\times0.08\\times2=1440$.","Compound: $9000\\times1.08^2=9000\\times1.1664=10497.60$, so the interest is $1497.60$.","Difference: $1497.60-1440=57.60$, the interest earned on the first year’s interest."],"answer":"Compound interest gives GH₵57.60 more.","model":null},{"q":"An item loses $20\\%$ of its current value every year. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w09">{"year":1,"week":9,"id":"y1w09","title":"Number Patterns, Algebraic Expressions and Factorisation","subtitle":"Turning patterns into general rules; terms, coefficients and like terms; expanding brackets; factorising by common factors, grouping and the difference of two squares.","family":"algebra","section":{"no":2,"name":"Algebra","strand":"Algebraic Reasoning","from":9,"to":12},"outcomes":["Describe a number or shape pattern with a general rule for the $n$th term.","Simplify algebraic expressions by collecting like terms and removing brackets.","Expand products of brackets, including squares of binomials.","Factorise by taking out common factors, by grouping and by the difference of two squares.","Check factorisations by expanding, and use algebra to model real situations."],"keywords":["variable","constant","term","coefficient","like terms","expression","equation","nth term","expand","factorise","grouping","difference of two squares"],"notes":[{"title":"The language of algebra","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **algebraic expression** describes a quantity using numbers, letters and operations. A **variable** is a letter that stands for a number that can change or is not yet known; a **constant** is a fixed number."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Terms and coefficients","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A **term** is a part of an expression separated by $+$ or $-$ signs. In $3x^2-5x+7$ the terms are $3x^2$, $-5x$ and $7$.","The **coefficient** is the number multiplying the variable part: the coefficient of $x$ in $-5x$ is $-5$.","Multiplication is often not written: $4ab$ means $4\\times a\\times b$."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Powers apply only to what they touch","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$5x^2$ means $5\\times x^2$, but $(5x)^2=5x\\times5x=25x^2$. An **expression** has no equals sign, e.g. $3x+1$. You **simplify** an expression; you **solve** an equation."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"From patterns to general rules","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Patterns help us predict how many objects a growing design needs. Suppose the first three figures have 5, 8 and 11 dots."},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-dots","caption":"Each figure keeps the same 2 grey dots and adds a column of 3 dots, so Figure $n$ has $3n+2$ dots."},{"k":"p","text":"The difference between terms is always $3$, so the rule has the form $T_n=3n+c$. Using $T_1=5$: $3(1)+c=5$, so $c=2$ and"},{"k":"math","tex":"T_n=3n+2"},{"k":"p","text":"Always test the rule on the given figures: $T_2=3(2)+2=8$ ✓ and $T_3=3(3)+2=11$ ✓."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"The $n$th term of a pattern with a constant difference","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"T_n=a+(n-1)d"},{"k":"p","text":"$a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference."}]},{"k":"p","text":"When the differences are not constant, look at how the shape grows in two directions. Rectangular arrangements often involve $n(n+1)$ or $n^2$; triangular dot patterns involve $\\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"State what $n$ can be","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In real contexts $n$ is usually a positive whole number (a figure number, a number of seats or of parcels). Say so, because negative or fractional values may make no sense."}]}],"figs":["w09-dots"]},{"title":"Simplifying expressions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Like terms** have exactly the same variable part, including the powers. $7x^2$ and $-2x^2$ are like terms; $7x^2$ and $7x$ are not."},{"k":"math","tex":"6a^2+3a-2a^2+5a=4a^2+8a"},{"k":"p","text":"To remove a bracket, use the **distributive law**: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Subtracting a bracket","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of **every** term inside:"},{"k":"math","tex":"7x-(3x-4)=7x-3x+4=4x+4"}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Expanding products of brackets","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To multiply two brackets, multiply **every** term in the first bracket by **every** term in the second. Each cell is a row term times a column term."},{"k":"math","tex":"(2x+3)(x-4)=2x^2-8x+3x-12=2x^2-5x-12"},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Useful identities","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$","$(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$","$(a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2$"]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Do not forget the middle term","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$(x+5)^2=(x+5)(x+5)=x^2+10x+25$, **not** $x^2+25$. Always look for a **common factor** first:"},{"k":"math","tex":"12x^2y-18xy^2=6xy(2x-3y)"},{"k":"p","text":"Check by expanding: $6xy\\times2x=12x^2y$ and $6xy\\times(-3y)=-18xy^2$ ✓."},{"k":"p","text":"**Grouping.** With four terms, pair them so that each pair has a common factor, then take out the common bracket:"},{"k":"math","tex":"ax+ay+bx+by=a(x+y)+b(x+y)=(a+b)(x+y)"},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-grouping","caption":"The four areas $ax$, $ay$, $bx$ and $by$ fit together into one rectangle of width $x+y$ and height $a+b$."},{"k":"p","text":"**Difference of two squares.** A perfect square minus a perfect square factorises as"},{"k":"math","tex":"a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)"},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $9x^2-16=(3x)^2-4^2=(3x-4)(3x+4)$."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"A sum of squares does not factorise this way","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$9x^2+16$ is a **sum** of two squares. Plan B: $10+8n$ cedis ($n$ a whole number).","Equal when $18+6n=10+8n$, so $8=2n$ and $n=4$.","For 10 parcels: A $=18+60=78$ and B $=10+80=90$."],"answer":"The costs are equal at 4 parcels; for 10 parcels Plan A is cheaper by GH₵12.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 9","items":["$n$th term of a pattern with common difference $d$: $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.","Like terms have the same variable part; a minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside.","$(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$ and $(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$","$a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$","Grouping: $ax+ay+bx+by=(a+b)(x+y)$"]}],"quiz":[{"q":"The terms $5x^2$, $-3x$ and $8$ belong to which expression?","options":["$5x^2-3x+8$","$5x^2\\times(-3x)\\times8$","$5(x^2-3x+8)$","$5x^2-3x-8$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Terms are separated by $+$ and $-$ signs: $5x^2$, $-3x$ and $+8$."},{"q":"A pattern is $4,\\ 9,\\ 14,\\ 19,\\ \\ldots$ What is its $n$th term?","options":["$4n+1$","$5n-1$","$5n+1$","$n+4$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$a=4$ and $d=5$: $T_n=4+5(n-1)=5n-1$."},{"q":"Simplify $7x-[3x-(2x-5)]$.","options":["$2x-5$","$6x+5$","$6x-5$","$12x-5$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Inner bracket: $3x-2x+5=x+5$.
